prompt: Ana writes `/notes.txt` in a container, runs `docker stop`, then `docker start`. Is the file there?
hint: Stopping ends the process. What about the layer?

choices.text: No, stopping a container wipes its writable layer, like a reboot does to RAM
choices.why: The layer is kept; `cat` printed `first note` after the start.

choices.text: Yes
choices.why: Right. A stopped container keeps its writable layer; only removal deletes it.

choices.text: Only if she committed it to an image first
choices.why: No commit is needed for a stop and start.

choices.text: Only if the container was started with `--rm`
choices.why: `--rm` does the opposite: it removes the container when it stops.

prompt: After `docker rm -f notes`, Ana runs `docker run -d --name notes alpine:3.22 sleep 3600` again and the file is missing. Why does reusing the name not bring it back?

choices.text: Names are reserved for an hour after removal
choices.why: The name was reused at once; it is just a label on a new container.

choices.text: The image was updated on Docker Hub in between the two runs
choices.why: The same image was used both times.

choices.text: The old layer went with the old container
choices.why: Right: the new one is a different container. The name is a label, not the container.

choices.text: Alpine clears `/` each time it starts
choices.why: The file survived a stop and start of the same container.

prompt: Match each letter in `docker diff` output to its meaning.
hint: Three letters, three kinds of change.
right_distractors: The path was copied from the image

prompt: `docker ps` shows nothing, yet the disk keeps filling. Which command would reveal containers that still hold writable layers?

choices.text: `docker image ls`, which lists every layer on the machine
choices.why: It lists images, not containers' writable layers.

choices.text: `docker diff` with no argument
choices.why: `diff` needs a container, which is what we are looking for.

choices.text: `docker volume ls`
choices.why: Volumes are separate from writable layers.

choices.text: `docker ps -a`
choices.why: Right. It also lists stopped containers, each with its layer.

prompt: Where was the `loans` table of the first `db` container actually stored?

choices.text: In an anonymous volume Docker created for it
choices.why: Right, which is why it could be rescued later.

choices.text: In the container's writable layer
choices.why: The image declares `/var/lib/postgresql/data` a volume, so the data went there instead.

choices.text: In the `postgres:17` image
choices.why: Images are read-only; containers never write into them.

choices.text: On Docker Hub, which backs up database containers
choices.why: Nothing about a container's data leaves the machine.

prompt: The second `db` container, started with the same command, had an empty database. Why?
hint: What did Docker mount for it?

choices.text: PostgreSQL deletes its data when it receives `SIGKILL`
choices.why: The data was still on disk and was read back later.

choices.text: It was given a new anonymous volume, which was empty
choices.why: Right. Nothing told Docker to reuse the first one.

choices.text: The first container's volume was deleted by `docker rm -f`
choices.why: It survived; Ana mounted it into `rescued`.

choices.text: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` resets the database each time
choices.why: The password only matters when the data directory is empty.

prompt: A week later Bruno runs `docker volume prune` to free disk space, with no container using the first anonymous volume. What happens to the rescued loans data if Ana had not mounted it again?
hint: What does prune remove by default?

choices.text: It is kept, because volumes are never pruned
choices.why: Prune exists to remove unused volumes.

choices.text: It is moved into the image
choices.why: Nothing moves data into images.

choices.text: It is deleted
choices.why: Right: prune removes anonymous volumes no container uses, which is what an orphaned database is.

choices.text: It is archived to `/var/lib/docker/trash`
choices.why: There is no such archive; removal is final.

prompt: To make every new database container reuse the same data, give the volume a name: `docker run -v ___:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17`, where the blank is a name such as `pgdata`. What kind of volume is that called?
Put Ana's rescue of the vanished table in order.
hint: Find it, free it, mount it, read it.
items: List the volumes and see two anonymous ones
Inspect the running `db` to learn which volume it uses
Remove `db`, so nothing else is using PostgreSQL's data
Start a new container with the other volume mounted on `/var/lib/postgresql/data`

prompt: Match each kind of state to where the lesson says it belongs.
hint: Only one of them may live in the writable layer.

pairs.right: A secret file, never the image
Standard output, collected by the engine

prompt: `docker history notes:snapshot` describes the committed layer as `sleep 3600`. What problem does that reveal?

choices.text: The commit failed and the file is missing
choices.why: The file is in the image; the history just does not say how.

choices.text: `sleep` cannot run in an image
choices.why: It is only the command the container happened to run.

choices.text: Commits are limited to 8.19kB
choices.why: That was simply the size of this layer.

choices.text: The image records nothing about how the file was made, so it cannot be rebuilt or reviewed
choices.why: Right. A Dockerfile writes the steps down; a commit does not.

prompt: When is `docker commit` the right tool?

choices.text: To keep a broken container's state as evidence
choices.why: Right: as evidence of what went wrong, not as something to run.

choices.text: To ship a new version of the application to production
choices.why: A release needs a recipe someone can rebuild; that is a Dockerfile.

choices.text: To back up a database container every night at the same hour
choices.why: The data belongs in a volume, and volumes have their own backups (lesson 8).

choices.text: To change a running container's configuration
choices.why: Configuration is set when a container is created; commit captures files.

prompt: Before removing a long-running container, which checks tell Ana whether anything will be lost? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Whether `docker diff` lists anything that matters
choices.why: Yes: that is the writable layer, which goes with the container.

choices.text: Whether its mounts include an anonymous volume
choices.why: Yes: it will be orphaned, and later pruned.

choices.text: Whether the image is the newest tag
choices.why: The image is not what is lost; it stays.

choices.text: Whether a new container with the same image and options would give the same result
choices.why: Yes: if not, something lives only in this one.

prompt: After `docker stop notes`, the status says `Exited (137)`. What does the 137 mean here?

choices.text: The container ran out of memory while it was sleeping
choices.why: Nothing used memory; `sleep` was waiting.

choices.text: `sleep` ignored the polite signal, then was killed
choices.why: Right: SIGKILL, signal 9, after ten seconds. Lesson 11 explains why.

choices.text: Docker's internal error code for any stopped container
choices.why: It is the process's exit status, 128 plus the signal.

choices.text: The file `/notes.txt` was 137 bytes
choices.why: Exit codes are not sizes.

prompt: Ana runs a throwaway PostgreSQL with `docker run --rm -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=x postgres:17` and stops it. What happens to the anonymous volume it used?
hint: What does `--rm` clean up besides the container?

choices.text: It stays, orphaned, like the ones in this lesson
choices.why: That happens with `docker rm`; `--rm` also removes anonymous volumes.

choices.text: It is renamed after the container
choices.why: Anonymous volumes keep their hash until they are removed.

choices.text: It is removed along with the container
choices.why: Right. `--rm` cleans up the container's anonymous volumes too.

choices.text: It is committed into the image
choices.why: Nothing writes into an image.
